Neonates of the Koa Tao Island caecilian (Ichthyophis kohtaoensis) emerge from their gelatinous egg masses following an incubation period of approximately 75 days [ab = approximately 75 days] when maintained at a constant temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. At the moment of eclosion, the freshly hatched larva measures about 7 cm [Lb = about 7 cm] in total length and carries a modest wet weight of 1.9 grams [Wwb = 1.9 grams], a value consistent with the computed allometric scaling from adult body dimensions. This relatively small size at hatching is typical of caecilians that exhibit extended parental attendance, as the yolk-dependent larva must rely entirely on endogenous reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The lecithotrophic stage is a critical phase during which the tiny larvae remain within or near the nest site, gradually absorbing the yolk material while undergoing early organogenesis. The relatively brief incubation period, combined with the small hatchling mass, suggests that Ichthyophis kohtaoensis invests in a moderately fast developmental tempo early in life, a pattern that contrasts with some of its larger-bodied congeneric relatives that produce fewer but larger neonates.

Field surveys and laboratory rearing studies have documented a predictable sequence of developmental milestones in Ichthyophis kohtaoensis when animals are kept under stable thermal conditions. At 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the free-swimming larva attains the metamorphic climax after a period of roughly 335 days following birth , a duration that encompasses both the endotrophic and early exotrophic phases of larval life. By the time of metamorphosis, the individual has reached a total length of 15 cm  and a corresponding wet weight of 19 grams , reflecting the substantial somatic growth achieved during the aquatic tadpole stage. The transition from a gill-breathing aquatic larva to a terrestrial juvenile involves profound morphological transformations, including the resorption of the tail fin and the development of a more robust, keratinised skin suited for a fossorial existence. This allometric shift in body plan reorganisation is energetically costly and is thought to be mediated by thyroid hormone cascades similar to those documented in other gymnophionan amphibians.

Reproductive maturation in Ichthyophis kohtaoensis follows a protracted timeline relative to its larval period. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation and the capacity for gametogenesis, occurs at approximately 2 years since birth [tp = approximately 2 years since birth] when individuals are reared at a constant 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. At this stage, the maturing individual has achieved a total length of 20 cm [Lp = 20 cm] and a wet weight of 44 grams [Wwp = 44 grams], indicating that a substantial portion of adult body size is attained before the reproductive system becomes fully active. The attainment of sexual maturity is not abrupt but appears to involve a gradual activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, with males typically maturing slightly earlier than females in captive colonies. This size-based threshold is consistent with observations in other ichthyophiid caecilians, where the onset of reproductive activity is tightly coupled to the achievement of a minimum body dimension rather than a strict chronological age alone.

Adult females of Ichthyophis kohtaoensis ultimately reach a maximum total length of 40 cm [Li = 40 cm], a value that represents the largest recorded specimens, although some earlier accounts by Manthey and Grossmann in 1997 reported a somewhat smaller figure of 28 cm for this sex. Males, in contrast, attain a slightly more modest ultimate length of 36.8 cm [Li = 36.8 cm], reflecting a moderate degree of sexual dimorphism in this species. The ultimate wet weight of the largest adult females has been estimated at 356 grams [Wwi = 356 grams] based on volumetric analysis of photographic material, a mass that underscores the robust, muscular body plan characteristic of fossorial caecilians. This substantial adult body mass, combined with a relatively elongated lifespan, sets the stage for a reproductive strategy that balances moderate clutch sizes against extended parental investment. The maximum recorded longevity under captive conditions at 23 °C [T = 23 °C] is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years], a lifespan that is considerable for an amphibian of this size and places Ichthyophis kohtaoensis among the longer-lived members of its genus.

Reproduction in Ichthyophis kohtaoensis is characterised by a moderate reproductive output that reflects its life-history strategy as a relatively large-bodied, long-lived caecilian. Females produce an average of 27 eggs per brood [N_R_i = 27 eggs per brood], and the maximum reproductive rate under optimal captive conditions at 23 °C [T = 23 °C] is approximately 0.13 broods per day [F_R_i = approximately 0.13 broods per day], a frequency that is high for a brooding caecilian and indicates a capacity for rapid sequential reproductive events when conditions are favorable. This comparatively high reproductive frequency, combined with a moderate brood size, suggests that under optimal conditions the species can produce many offspring per year, a strategy that may be adaptive in its seasonal tropical habitat.
